questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented for a new patient appointment. She had been diagnosed with HIV 3 years earlier and was established on ART . Investigations: CD4 count 550 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable Annual Pap smears for past 3 years: normal cytology
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Co-testing of HPV with next Pap smear
Repeat cervical cytology testing in 3 years
Repeat cervical cytology testing in 5 years

questions.explanation: Repeat cervical cytology testing in 3 years Cervical cancer is considered an AIDS-defining illness, because of the higher rates seen among persons infected with HIV with advanced disease. The etiology for this is likely due to more difficulty in clearing HPV infection due to immunosuppression among those infected. Current guidelines for screening HIV-infected women are based upon age. It is recommended that all women undergo screening upon initiation of care. For women less than 30 years of age (as with this patient), it is recommended to screen at 12-month intervals for 3 years if results remain normal and then every 3 years thereafter. If atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) are seen with positive HPV testing, colposcopy is recommended with repeat cytology at 6–12 months. If low-grade squamous epithelial lesions (LSIL) and higher, colposcopy should be performed. Co-testing is not recommended in this age group for HPV . For women 30 years and older, cervical cytology with or without co-testing with HPV should be done every 12 months for 3 consecutive years and, if normal, then every 3 years thereafter. For ASCUS results with positive HPV testing, management is the same as above. For LSIL and higher, recommendations are the same as above. However, for women who receive co-testing where cytology is negative and HPV is positive, it is recommended to repeat co-testing in 1 year (unless genotypes 16/18, in which colposcopy is recommended). If either of the co-test is abnormal at 1 year, then colposcopy should be performed. HPV vaccine is recommended for young women only up until age 26.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q37

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male presented to the student health clinic with about a week of fevers, malaise, sore throat, oral ulcers, and one day of nonpruritic, diffuse, erythematous morbilliform rash. He is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. He is sexually active. On exam, he has nonexudative pharyngitis with stomatitis, along with palpable cervical lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly.
questions.lead_in: In addition to testing for infectious mononucleosis, you should also consider what diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute HIV infection Acute HIV can present with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and exanthematous rash and should be considered in the differential diagnosis when a patient presents with a mononucleosis-like syndrome.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q30

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, and a rash. On examination she had a maculopapular rash and generalized lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL AST 65 units/L ALT 96 units/L Bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL EBV IgM positive, IgG positive, EBNA positive HIV Ab/Ag test negative HIV viral load 1.2 million copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine +atazanavir/ cobicistat Initiation of ART in symptomatic acute HIV reduces symptoms and is now recommended. As a HLA B*5701 result is not available, abacavir-based regimens should be avoided. In the setting of acute infection, resistance assays may not be readily available, as in this case. In the absence of a resistance assay a protease-based or dolutegravir-based regimen is recommended pending results. Tenofovir alafenamide+cobicis tat+elvitegravir is incorrect as it is an incomplete regimen.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q21

questions.question: A woman with acute HIV seroconversion. CD4 550.
questions.question_raw: PM Q3. Woman with acute HIV seroconversion. CD4 550.

parts.text: What are the treatment benefits of initiating therapy right away?

parts_raw.text: a) What treatment should you start?
b) What are the treatment benefits of initiating therapy right away?

questions.model_answer:
a) Start an INSTI-based regimen with a dual-NRTI backbone immediately (send resistance testing and HLA-B*5701 but do not wait): dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)-emtricitabine, or coformulated bictegravir-TAF-emtricitabine; raltegravir + tenofovir-emtricitabine, or dolutegravir-abacavir-lamivudine if HLA-B*5701 negative, are the other recommended options.
b) (1) Acute or recent HIV infection is an explicit condition favoring early initiation, and ART is now recommended universally regardless of CD4 count. (2) Maximal and durable suppression of plasma HIV RNA to <50 copies/mL. (3) Preservation and restoration of immune function (CD4 rise of 50-150 cells/mm3 in year 1, with near-normal counts achievable when started above 350). (4) Reduced HIV-related morbidity and mortality. (5) Prevention of onward transmission (96% reduction with early ART in HPTN 052).

cohort_answer.text:
DTG + Tenofovir + Emtricitabine (AI); DTG + Abacavir + Lamivudine (AI, if HLA B5701 negative); Bictegravir + TAF + Emtricitabine (AI); Raltegravir + TDF + Emtricitabine (BI)
Maximally and durably suppress plasma HIV RNA; Restore and preserve immunologic function; Reduce HIV-associated morbidity and prolong duration/quality of survival; Prevent HIV transmission

questions.question: A man who has sex with men and injects drugs presents with fever, splenomegaly, and rash.
questions.question_raw: Homosexual IVDU with fever, splenomegaly, rash
questions.model_answer: a) Differential: (1) Acute HIV (retroviral syndrome) - fever, rash, splenomegaly; consider HIV-associated opportunistic causes (Bartonella henselae/quintana, disseminated salmonellosis). (2) Infective endocarditis (injection-related, typically S. aureus; right-sided) with embolic/immunologic phenomena. (3) Secondary syphilis (diffuse rash including palms/soles). (4) Acute viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV) or mononucleosis-type infection (EBV, CMV, acute toxoplasmosis). (5) Other: disseminated gonococcemia, rickettsial infection, acute HBV serum-sickness; non-infectious mimics (drug reaction, Still disease, SLE). b) (1) Admit; standard/contact precautions as indicated. (2) Blood cultures x3, HIV Ag/Ab and viral load (p24/RNA for acute window), RPR/treponemal serology, hepatitis B/C serologies, EBV/CMV, Bartonella serology. (3) Echocardiography (TTE then TEE) for endocarditis. (4) Imaging: abdominal ultrasound/CT for splenomegaly/abscess; CXR. (5) Empiric antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin +/- ceftriaxone) if endocarditis/sepsis suspected, after cultures. (6) Dermatology assessment of rash; treat syphilis if confirmed. (7) Harm-reduction counselling, addiction/social work referral, and HIV linkage-to-care if positive.
questions.beyond_mandell: Broad DDx/management drawn from general ID practice and IDSA guidance; this vignette is outside the endocarditis chapter scope.

cohort_answer.text: DDx: HIV (primary/acute retroviral syndrome; immunocompromised - Bartonella henselae/quintana, non-typhoidal Salmonella); secondary syphilis; endocarditis, HepC; EBV, CMV, Toxoplasma gondii, TB (erythema nodosum), early disseminated Lyme, Rickettsia, Typhoid, Chlamydia psittaci, Visceral Leish; non-infectious (SLE, Still's, drug reactions); multifactorial (HLH, cirrhosis). Management: Admit to hospital, IPAC precautions as needed, investigations (HIV p24/VL, blood cultures, serologies - syphilis/EBV/CMV/Toxo/Bartonella/HepB/C/Lyme, echo, abdo US, TST/CXR, derm consult), empiric antibiotics (CTX/vanco) if endocarditis concern, HIV follow-up if positive, harm reduction counselling/social work

needs: Chapter 131 — Management of Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.question: A patient is started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
questions.question_raw: A patient is started on HAART.

parts.text: Explain the pathogenesis of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

questions.model_answer:
a) Potent ART rapidly suppresses HIV-1 RNA and raises CD4+ counts, producing at least partial immune reconstitution with return of pathogen-specific T-cell responses. Because recovery of antigen-specific immunity lags behind the CD4 rise and is dysregulated, the restored inflammatory response is directed against antigens of a persisting or recently treated pathogen (or its residual antigen), producing paradoxical clinical worsening of a previously silent, subclinical or adequately treated opportunistic infection (paradoxical IRIS) or unmasking of an undiagnosed one (unmasking IRIS). These reversal/unmasking reactions are analogous to reversal reactions in multibacillary leprosy: fever, focal lymphadenitis, worsening infiltrates or new inflammatory lesions typically 1 to 3 weeks (up to 1-2 months) after ART initiation. It is inflammation, not treatment failure; drug resistance, nonadherence, malabsorption, lymphoma and drug reaction must be excluded. Classically described with mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex), and also with Cryptococcus neoformans, Pneumocystis jirovecii, PML, CMV (immune recovery uveitis/vitritis), Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma; CNS IRIS carries the highest morbidity and mortality.
b) (1) Recent initiation of ART with a marked virologic/immunologic response (worsening typically within 2-3 weeks of starting therapy). (2) An underlying opportunistic infection with high antigen burden, particularly active or recently treated tuberculosis (incidence of tuberculosis IRIS 7%-43%), and, by extension, advanced immunosuppression with a low baseline CD4+ count.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell states IRIS risk factors are "not well understood"; low baseline CD4 count, high pre-ART viral load, high pathogen burden and short interval between OI treatment and ART start come from DHHS/IDSA opportunistic infection guidance.
